references.label: NG39 restrictive
references.citation: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence. Major trauma: assessment and initial management (NG39). 2016.
references.excerpt: For patients with active bleeding use a restrictive approach to volume resuscitation until definitive early control of bleeding has been achieved.

references.label: NG39 TBI and shock
references.citation: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence. Major trauma: assessment and initial management (NG39). 2016.
references.excerpt: if haemorrhagic shock is the dominant condition, continue restrictive volume resuscitation or if traumatic brain injury is the dominant condition, use a less restrictive volume resuscitation approach to maintain cerebral perfusion.

references.label: Rossaint 2023 lactate
references.citation: Rossaint R, Afshari A, Bouillon B, et al. The European guideline on management of major bleeding and coagulopathy following trauma: sixth edition. Crit Care. 2023;27:80.
references.excerpt: We recommend blood lactate as a sensitive test to estimate and monitor the extent of bleeding and tissue hypoperfusion; in the absence of lactate measurements, base deficit may represent a suitable alternative (Grade 1B).

references.label: Rossaint 2023 BP target
references.citation: Rossaint R, Afshari A, Bouillon B, et al. The European guideline on management of major bleeding and coagulopathy following trauma: sixth edition. Crit Care. 2023;27:80.
references.excerpt: In the initial phase following trauma, we recommend the use of a restricted volume replacement strategy with a target systolic blood pressure of 80–90 mmHg (mean arterial pressure 50–60 mmHg) until major bleeding has been stopped without clinical evidence of brain injury (Grade 1B). In patients with severe TBI (GCS ≤ 8), we recommend that a mean arterial pressure ≥ 80 mmHg be maintained (Grade 1C).

references.label: Rossaint 2023 vasopressor
references.citation: Rossaint R, Afshari A, Bouillon B, et al. The European guideline on management of major bleeding and coagulopathy following trauma: sixth edition. Crit Care. 2023;27:80.
references.excerpt: If a restricted volume replacement strategy does not achieve the target blood pressure, we recommend the administration of noradrenaline in addition to fluids to maintain target arterial pressure (Grade 1C).

references.label: Rossaint 2023 haemoglobin
references.citation: Rossaint R, Afshari A, Bouillon B, et al. The European guideline on management of major bleeding and coagulopathy following trauma: sixth edition. Crit Care. 2023;27:80.
references.excerpt: If erythrocyte transfusion is necessary, we recommend a target haemoglobin of 70–90 g/L (Grade 1C).

references.label: Rossaint 2023 initial products
references.citation: Rossaint R, Afshari A, Bouillon B, et al. The European guideline on management of major bleeding and coagulopathy following trauma: sixth edition. Crit Care. 2023;27:80.
references.excerpt: In the initial management of patients with expected massive haemorrhage, we recommend one of the two following strategies: Fibrinogen concentrate or cryoprecipitate and pRBC (Grade 1C) FFP or pathogen-inactivated FFP in a FFP/pRBC ratio of at least 1:2 as needed (Grade 1C) In addition, we suggest a high platelet/pRBC ratio (Grade 2B).

cards.question: In adult trauma with uncontrolled major bleeding, how does severe traumatic brain injury change the initial blood-pressure target?
cards.answer: Without clinical evidence of brain injury, use restricted volume replacement and aim for a systolic pressure of 80–90 mmHg until bleeding is controlled. With severe traumatic brain injury (GCS 8 or less), maintain a mean arterial pressure of at least 80 mmHg. Source: European trauma bleeding guideline, sixth edition, recommendation 13.

cards.question: An adult trauma patient is bleeding or at risk of significant bleeding. When and how should tranexamic acid be given?
cards.answer: Start as soon as possible and within 3 hours of injury. Infuse 1 g IV over 10 minutes, followed by a second 1 g IV over 8 hours. Source: European trauma bleeding guideline, sixth edition, recommendation 23.
